appraisal_events.evidence: Quel brave homme que votre père! ... Eux et lui, quelles bonnes gens! ... le duc de Guermantes n'eût pas eu d'hésitation à les recommander pour une place de jardiniers ... pour l'humilier. C'est ainsi qu'un antisémite dit à un Juif ... du mal des Juifs.
appraisal_events.explanation: The Guermantes couple's warm-sounding reminiscence about Swann's modest, 'honest' family is exposed by the narrator as condescension disguised as affability, the same rhetorical structure he compares to an antisemite's backhanded remarks to a Jew.

appraisal_events.evidence: Elle est spirituelle, c'est tout à fait le tour de son père. — Je trouve qu'elle lui est même très supérieure ... elle a un brio que Swann n'avait pas.
appraisal_events.explanation: After Gilberte's departure, the duke and duchess praise her wit as not merely inherited from Swann but surpassing his, an explicit comparative elevation delivered behind her back.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator explicitly names the Guermantes' fond talk of Swann's humble origins as a form of humiliation dressed as flattery.
His family's modest station is spoken of aloud, in front of his daughter, by the aristocratic hosts who once received him -- a witnessed, if genteel, lowering of his remembered standing.
The Guermantes explicitly rate her wit as superior to her father's, a clear local elevation delivered as private praise after her visit.
In the same comparison that elevates Gilberte, the duke insists Swann himself lacked her 'brio,' a milder, separately timed and partly contested diminishment of Swann.

ambiguities: The duke's claim that Swann 'n'avait pas de brio' is immediately preceded by the duchess insisting he was indeed very witty, so the comparative diminishment of Swann in E2 is only partial and disputed within the exchange itself.
